claim: Identical stimuli can be perceived or go unnoticed across successive presentations, producing divergent behavioral outcomes despite similarities in sensory input.
source: Identical stimuli can be perceived or go unnoticed across successive presentations, producing divergent behavioral outcomes despite similarities in sensory input.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about perceptual variability that is established in the field and forms the basis for the study.

claim: Hit trials were characterized by a behavioral state with heightened arousal.
source: Hit trials were characterized by a behavioral state with heightened arousal, greater eye position stability, and enhanced decoding performance of stimulus identity from neural activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by pupil diameter measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: Hit trials were characterized by greater eye position stability.
source: Hit trials were characterized by a behavioral state with heightened arousal, greater eye position stability, and enhanced decoding performance of stimulus identity from neural activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by microsaccade analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Hit trials were characterized by enhanced decoding performance of stimulus identity from neural activity.
source: Hit trials were characterized by a behavioral state with heightened arousal, greater eye position stability, and enhanced decoding performance of stimulus identity from neural activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by linear discriminant analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Target stimuli evoked stronger responses in V4 in hit trials.
source: Target stimuli evoked stronger responses in V4 in hit trials, and excitatory neurons in the superficial layers, the primary feed-forward output of the cortical column, exhibited lower variability.
evidence: This claim is supported by firing rate analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Excitatory neurons in the superficial layers exhibited lower variability in hit trials.
source: Target stimuli evoked stronger responses in V4 in hit trials, and excitatory neurons in the superficial layers, the primary feed-forward output of the cortical column, exhibited lower variability.
evidence: This claim is supported by Fano factor analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The superficial layers are the primary feed-forward output of the cortical column.
source: Target stimuli evoked stronger responses in V4 in hit trials, and excitatory neurons in the superficial layers, the primary feed-forward output of the cortical column, exhibited lower variability.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of cortical anatomy and connectivity.

claim: Feed-forward interlaminar population correlations were stronger on hits.
source: Feed-forward interlaminar population correlations were stronger on hits.
evidence: This claim is supported by canonical correlation analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Hit trials were characterized by greater synchrony between the output layers of the cortex during spontaneous activity.
source: Hit trials were further characterized by greater synchrony between the output layers of the cortex during spontaneous activity, while the stimulus-evoked period showed elevated synchrony in the feed-forward pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by spike-spike coherence analysis during the pre-stimulus period.

claim: The stimulus-evoked period showed elevated synchrony in the feed-forward pathway during hit trials.
source: Hit trials were further characterized by greater synchrony between the output layers of the cortex during spontaneous activity, while the stimulus-evoked period showed elevated synchrony in the feed-forward pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by spike-spike coherence analysis during the stimulus-evoked period.

claim: A state of elevated arousal and stable retinal images allow enhanced processing of sensory stimuli, which contributes to hits at perceptual threshold.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that a state of elevated arousal and stable retinal images allow enhanced processing of sensory stimuli, which contributes to hits at perceptual threshold.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion drawn from multiple experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Low-intensity stimuli are detected infrequently.
source: Physical properties of stimuli strongly influence perception such that low-intensity stimuli are detected infrequently.
evidence: This is established knowledge about psychophysics and perception.

claim: As stimulus intensity increases, detection probability remains low until some perceptual threshold is crossed, after which stimuli are perceived robustly.
source: As intensity increases, detection probability remains low until some perceptual threshold is crossed, after which stimuli are perceived robustly.
evidence: This is established knowledge about psychometric functions and perceptual thresholds.

claim: A psychometric function mathematically describes the property of perception where detection probability changes with stimulus intensity.
source: A psychometric function (Prins and Kingdom, 2018; Watson, 1979; Wichmann and Hill, 2001) mathematically describes this property of perception.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on psychometric functions.

claim: Only within a narrow range around the perceptual threshold do stimuli lead to significant trial-to-trial perceptual variance.
source: Only within a narrow range around the perceptual threshold do stimuli lead to significant trial-to-trial perceptual variance.
evidence: This is established knowledge about perceptual thresholds.

claim: Few studies have probed the laminar cortical microcircuit mechanisms that underlie successful or unsuccessful perception at threshold conditions.
source: While many studies present stimuli at threshold (Herman et al., 2019; Levitt, 1971; Pins and Ffytche, 2003; Ress and Heeger, 2003), few have probed the laminar cortical microcircuit mechanisms that underlie successful or unsuccessful perception under these conditions (McCormick et al., 2020; van Vugt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Perceived stimuli trigger stronger information propagation from earlier visual areas to higher-order visual and frontal regions.
source: Prior studies have characterized how perceived stimuli trigger stronger information propagation from earlier visual areas to higher-order visual and frontal regions (Herman et al., 2019; van Vugt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Information propagation and sensory processing are strongly influenced by brain states such as arousal and attention.
source: This information propagation and sensory processing are strongly influenced by brain states such as arousal and attention (McCormick et al., 2020; Harris and Thiele, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Arousal has long been recognized for its role in modulating cortical activity.
source: Arousal has long been recognized for its role in modulating cortical activity (Livingstone and Hubel, 1981; McCormick and Bal, 1997; Vinck et al., 2015) and affecting performance in various sensory tasks (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; McGinley et al., 2015; Yerkes and Dodson, 1908).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Arousal affects performance in various sensory tasks.
source: Arousal has long been recognized for its role in modulating cortical activity (Livingstone and Hubel, 1981; McCormick and Bal, 1997; Vinck et al., 2015) and affecting performance in various sensory tasks (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; McGinley et al., 2015; Yerkes and Dodson, 1908).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Visual area V4 is a key intermediate region in the ventral visual processing stream.
source: In visual area V4, a key intermediate region in the ventral visual processing stream (Goodale and Milner, 1992; Mountcastle, 1997; Roe et al., 2012), attention strongly modulates neural activity (Desimone and Duncan, 1995; McAdams and Maunsell, 1999; Moran and Desimone, 1985; Reynolds et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on visual processing streams.

claim: Attention strongly modulates neural activity in V4.
source: In visual area V4, a key intermediate region in the ventral visual processing stream (Goodale and Milner, 1992; Mountcastle, 1997; Roe et al., 2012), attention strongly modulates neural activity (Desimone and Duncan, 1995; McAdams and Maunsell, 1999; Moran and Desimone, 1985; Reynolds et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on attentional modulation in V4.

claim: Attention increases the firing rates of V4 neurons.
source: Attention increases the firing rates of V4 neurons, enhances the reliability of individual neuron firing, and reduces correlated fluctuations among pairs of neurons (McAdams and Maunsell, 1999; Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Mitchell et al., 2007; Mitchell et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Attention enhances the reliability of individual neuron firing in V4.
source: Attention increases the firing rates of V4 neurons, enhances the reliability of individual neuron firing, and reduces correlated fluctuations among pairs of neurons (McAdams and Maunsell, 1999; Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Mitchell et al., 2007; Mitchell et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Attention reduces correlated fluctuations among pairs of neurons in V4.
source: Attention increases the firing rates of V4 neurons, enhances the reliability of individual neuron firing, and reduces correlated fluctuations among pairs of neurons (McAdams and Maunsell, 1999; Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Mitchell et al., 2007; Mitchell et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Brain state dynamics impact both cortical and subcortical structures, contributing to behavior.
source: Brain state dynamics impact both cortical and subcortical structures, contributing to behavior (Ghosh and Maunsell, 2021; Zénon and Krauzlis, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Fluctuations in attention are reflected in the on- and off-state dynamics of V4 ensembles.
source: Fluctuations in attention are reflected in the on- and off-state dynamics of V4 ensembles, which have been shown to correlate with behavioral performance (Engel et al., 2016; van Kempen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: On- and off-state dynamics of V4 ensembles correlate with behavioral performance.
source: Fluctuations in attention are reflected in the on- and off-state dynamics of V4 ensembles, which have been shown to correlate with behavioral performance (Engel et al., 2016; van Kempen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The visual cortex has a columnar architecture in which multiple cell classes across the cortical layers form distinct sub-populations.
source: The visual cortex has a columnar architecture in which multiple cell classes (Connors and Gutnick, 1990; Markram et al., 2004; Migliore and Shepherd, 2005; Wonders and Anderson, 2006; Zeng and Sanes, 2017) across the cortical layers (Mountcastle, 1997; Douglas and Martin, 2004) form distinct sub-populations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on cortical architecture.

claim: Cortical sub-populations have unique and stereotyped patterns of connectivity, forming a canonical microcircuit that orchestrates the encoding and flow of information.
source: These sub-populations have unique and stereotyped patterns of connectivity, thus forming a canonical microcircuit that orchestrates the encoding and flow of information (Douglas and Martin, 2007; Hirsch and Martinez, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on cortical microcircuits.

claim: Cortical sub-populations contribute uniquely to sensory processing and are differentially modulated by brain states.
source: Moreover, these sub-populations contribute uniquely to sensory processing and are differentially modulated by brain states (Mitchell et al., 2007; Nandy et al., 2017; McCormick et al., 1985; Pettine et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Attentional modulation varies across cortical layers.
source: While it has been shown that attentional modulation varies across cortical layers (Nandy et al., 2017; Pettine et al., 2019; Mehta et al., 2000a; Mehta et al., 2000b; Buffalo et al., 2011; Ferro et al., 2021; Westerberg et al., 2021; Westerberg et al., 2022), the role of these sub-populations in attentive perception at threshold remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The role of cortical sub-populations in attentive perception at threshold remains poorly understood.
source: While it has been shown that attentional modulation varies across cortical layers (Nandy et al., 2017; Pettine et al., 2019; Mehta et al., 2000a; Mehta et al., 2000b; Buffalo et al., 2011; Ferro et al., 2021; Westerberg et al., 2021; Westerberg et al., 2022), the role of these sub-populations in attentive perception at threshold remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The influence of physiological states on cortical sub-populations has not been studied in detail.
source: Moreover, the influence of physiological states, which may be responsible for different outcomes at threshold, on these sub-populations has not been studied in detail.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Minor fluctuations in behavioral state, such as arousal and visual sensitivity, and in the activity of neural sub-populations across the layers of the visual cortex, result in different perceptual outcomes at threshold.
source: We hypothesized that minor fluctuations in behavioral state, such as arousal and visual sensitivity, and in the activity of neural sub-populations across the layers of the visual cortex, result in different perceptual outcomes at threshold.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the study.

claim: Output layer sub-populations projecting to higher cortical areas and subcortical structures would show evidence of improved capacity for stimulus representation during successful perception.
source: Specifically, we hypothesized that output layer (II–III, V–VI) sub-populations, ones projecting to higher cortical areas and subcortical structures, would show evidence of improved capacity for stimulus representation during successful perception.
evidence: This is a specific hypothesis of the study.

claim: Successful perceptual events would be accompanied by improved information propagation throughout a cortical column.
source: We also hypothesized that such successful events would be accompanied by improved information propagation throughout a cortical column.
evidence: This is a specific hypothesis of the study.

claim: Differences in behavioral states and lamina-specific neural states characterize correct and incorrect trials at threshold and explain perceptual variability.
source: We find that differences in behavioral states and lamina-specific neural states characterize correct and incorrect trials at threshold and explain perceptual variability.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Monkeys were trained to detect an orientation change in one of two Gabor stimuli that were presented concurrently at two spatial locations.
source: Monkeys were trained to detect an orientation change in one of two Gabor stimuli that were presented concurrently at two spatial locations, and to report having seen the change by making an eye movement to the changed stimulus.
evidence: This describes the experimental task design.

claim: Monkeys were cued as to which of the two spatial locations was likely to undergo the orientation change with 95% validity.
source: Prior to a block of trials, monkeys were cued as to which of the two spatial locations was likely to undergo the orientation change (95% valid cue; presented at the start of each block).
evidence: This describes the experimental task design.

claim: Non-target stimuli at a fixed reference orientation were repeatedly presented during a trial.
source: During a trial, 'non-target' stimuli at a fixed reference orientation were repeatedly presented.
evidence: This describes the experimental task design.

claim: Non-target stimuli were turned on for 200 ms and then turned off for a variable interval of 200–400 ms.
source: Non-targets were turned on for 200 ms at the two spatial locations, and then turned off for a variable interval (200–400 ms).
evidence: This describes the experimental task design.

claim: A target stimulus, differing in orientation from the non-targets, was presented at a random time between 1–5 s (mean 3 s).
source: At a random time (1–5 s, mean 3 s) a 'target' stimulus, differing in orientation from the non-targets, was presented at one of the locations.
evidence: This describes the experimental task design.

claim: If the monkey reported having detected the orientation change by making an eye movement to the location of the target stimulus, it received a juice reward (hit trial).
source: If the monkey reported having detected the orientation change by making an eye movement to the location of the target stimulus, it received a juice reward (Figure 1A, 'hit' trial).
evidence: This describes the experimental task design and trial classification.

claim: If the monkey failed to detect the orientation change and instead continued to maintain fixation on the center of the monitor, it was not rewarded (miss trial).
source: If the monkey failed to detect the orientation change and instead continued to maintain fixation on the center of the monitor, it was not rewarded (Figure 1A, 'miss' trial).
evidence: This describes the experimental task design and trial classification.

claim: The study focused exclusively on trials in which the target stimulus was presented at the cued location (95% of trials).
source: In this study, we focused exclusively on trials in which the target stimulus was presented at the cued location (95% of trials).
evidence: This describes the data selection criteria for analysis.

claim: The threshold condition was defined as the orientation change that was closest to the 50% threshold of the fitted psychometric function for that session.
source: We fit the behavioral data with a logistic function (Prins and Kingdom, 2018) and defined the threshold condition as the orientation change that was closest to the 50% threshold of the fitted psychometric function for that session (Figure 1B, Materials and methods; see Figure 1—figure supplement 2 for additional examples and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–G for logistic fit parameters).
evidence: This describes the method for defining the threshold condition.

claim: Target presentation times were not different between hit and miss trials.
source: Target presentation times were not different between hit and miss trials (Figure 1—figure supplement 3H; p=0.15, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of target presentation times.

claim: There was a slight difference in threshold trial performance based on time in the session.
source: There was a slight difference in threshold trial performance based on time in the session (Figure 1—figure supplement 3I, p<0.01, permutation test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding about performance over time.

claim: Performance in the middle of the recording session (second and third quartiles) was higher than in the beginning and end of the session (first and fourth quartiles).
source: Performance in the middle of the recording session (second and third quartiles) was higher than in the beginning and end of the session (first and fourth quartiles).
evidence: This is a statistical finding about performance over time.

claim: Monkeys initiated a median of 905 trials per session (range: 651–1086).
source: Monkeys initiated a median of 905 trials per session (range: 651–1086).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic about the experimental sessions.

claim: Single- and multi-unit activity and local field potentials (LFPs) were recorded in area V4 using 16-channel linear array electrodes.
source: While monkeys performed this task, single- and multi-unit activity and local field potentials (LFPs) were recorded in area V4 using 16-channel linear array electrodes (Plexon Inc, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This describes the electrophysiological recording methods.

claim: The array was inserted perpendicular to the cortical surface and spanned the cortical layers.
source: The array was inserted perpendicular to the cortical surface and spanned the cortical layers.
evidence: This describes the electrophysiological recording methods.

claim: Single units were classified as either broad-spiking (putative excitatory neurons) or narrow-spiking (putative inhibitory neurons) on the basis of their waveform width.
source: Single units were classified as either broad-spiking (putative excitatory neurons) or narrow-spiking (putative inhibitory neurons) on the basis of their waveform width using previously published techniques (peak-to-trough duration; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D; see Materials and methods; Connors and Gutnick, 1990; Nandy et al., 2017; McCormick et al., 1985; Kawaguchi, 1993; Nowak et al., 2003).
evidence: This describes the method for cell type classification, supported by citations.

claim: Eye position and pupil diameter were recorded using ISCAN ETL-200.
source: Eye position and pupil diameter were also recorded (ISCAN ETL-200).
evidence: This describes the behavioral measurement methods.

claim: Larger pupil diameter is thought to be a proxy for elevated alertness and arousal.
source: Larger pupil diameter is thought to be a proxy for elevated alertness and arousal (McCormick et al., 2020; Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; McGinley et al., 2015; Beatty and Lucero-Wagoner, 2000; Hess and Polt, 1964; Reimer et al., 2014; Tang and Higley, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Hit trials were associated with larger pupil diameters compared to miss trials, both before and during non-target and target stimulus presentations.
source: We found that hit trials were associated with larger pupil diameters compared to miss trials, both before and during non-target and target stimulus presentations (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by pupil diameter measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The mean of the distribution of pupil diameters associated with hit trials is greater than that associated with misses.
source: We found that the mean of the distribution of pupil diameters associated with hit trials is greater than that associated with misses (Figure 2B; complementary null hypothesis testing results in Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The optimal state for sensory performance occurs at intermediate levels of arousal, with states of low and hyper arousal associated with decreased performance.
source: Prior work has shown that the optimal state for sensory performance occurs at intermediate levels of arousal, with states of low and hyper arousal associated with decreased performance (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; McGinley et al., 2015; Yerkes and Dodson, 1908; Cools and D'Esposito, 2011; Murphy et al., 2011; Rajagovindan and Ding, 2011; Vijayraghavan et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In both hit and miss trials, the mean pupil diameter was close to the optimal arousal state for perceptual performance.
source: In both hit and miss trials, the mean pupil diameter was close to the optimal arousal state for perceptual performance (Figure 2C; McGinley et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the distribution shown in Figure 2C and comparison to prior literature.

claim: The average differences in pupil diameter across hit and miss trials reflect differences within the optimal state of intermediate arousal.
source: The average differences in pupil diameter across hit and miss trials reflect differences within the optimal state of intermediate arousal.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the pupil diameter data in the context of arousal states.

claim: Hits are more likely to occur during periods of greater arousal.
source: Our results thus suggest that hits are more likely to occur during periods of greater arousal.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pupil diameter findings.

claim: Microsaccades are small fixational eye movements of <1° in amplitude that occur during normal fixation.
source: Microsaccades, small fixational eye movements of <1° in amplitude that occur during normal fixation, are associated with periods of decreased visual sensitivity due to unstable retinal images (Dicke et al., 2008; Zuber and Stark, 1966).
evidence: This is established knowledge about microsaccades, supported by citations.

claim: Microsaccades are associated with periods of decreased visual sensitivity due to unstable retinal images.
source: Microsaccades, small fixational eye movements of <1° in amplitude that occur during normal fixation, are associated with periods of decreased visual sensitivity due to unstable retinal images (Dicke et al., 2008; Zuber and Stark, 1966).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Microsaccades have been linked to suppressed neural responses in visual areas during perceptual tasks, impairing fine visual discrimination and behavioral performance.
source: Microsaccades have been linked to suppressed neural responses in visual areas during perceptual tasks, impairing fine visual discrimination and behavioral performance (Beeler, 1967; Hafed and Krauzlis, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Most trials with a pre-target microsaccade were misses, whereas the majority of trials without a microsaccade in the 400 ms window preceding target onset were hits.
source: Most trials with a pre-target microsaccade were misses, whereas the majority of trials without a microsaccade in this window were hits (Figure 2D; see Figure 2—figure supplement 2D for individual animal plots).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There is a strong link between microsaccade direction and attention deployment.
source: There is a strong link between microsaccade direction and attention deployment (Lowet et al., 2018; Engbert and Kliegl, 2003; Hafed and Clark, 2002; Gowen et al., 2007; Galfano et al., 2004; Pastukhov and Braun, 2010; Yu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Microsaccades toward the attended stimulus were overrepresented in correct trials.
source: Consistent with previous reports we also find that microsaccades toward the attended stimulus were overrepresented in correct trials (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, upper left).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Microsaccades toward the attended stimulus were underrepresented in incorrect trials.
source: Conversely, microsaccades toward the attended stimulus were underrepresented in incorrect trials (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, lower left).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There was a very low but statistically significant negative correlation between pupil diameter and microsaccade rate.
source: There was a very low but statistically significant negative correlation between pupil diameter and microsaccade rate (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, r2 = 0.006, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Successful trials at threshold are significantly more likely to occur during a state of greater arousal and improved visual sensitivity.
source: Overall, these results suggest that successful trials at threshold are significantly more likely to occur during a state of greater arousal and improved visual sensitivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pupil diameter and microsaccade findings.

claim: A linear decoder could better discriminate targets from non-targets in hits compared to misses.
source: A linear decoder could better discriminate targets from non-targets in hits compared to misses (Figure 3A; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for individual animal plots), suggesting differences in firing rates across these trial types.
evidence: This is supported by the decoding analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Improved stimulus discriminability in hits was consistent across all three cortical layers.
source: This improved stimulus discriminability was consistent across all three layers (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the decoding analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For non-target stimuli, firing rates were equivalent for hits and misses in both the pre-stimulus and stimulus-evoked periods.
source: For non-target stimuli, firing rates were equivalent for hits and misses in both the pre-stimulus (0–200 ms before stimulus onset) and stimulus-evoked (60–260 ms following stimulus onset) periods (Figure 3B; see Figure 3—figure supplement 2 for individual animal plots).
evidence: This is supported by the firing rate analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: For the target stimulus, firing rates were equivalent in the pre-stimulus period but hit trials were characterized by elevated firing across cortical layers in the stimulus-evoked period.
source: For the target stimulus, firing rates were once again equivalent in the pre-stimulus period, but hit trials were characterized by elevated firing across cortical layers in the stimulus-evoked period (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is supported by the firing rate analysis shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: Broad- and narrow-spiking neurons in both the input and deep layers respond more to target stimuli in hit trials.
source: Broad- and narrow-spiking neurons in both the input and deep layers respond more to target stimuli in hit trials, and trend toward elevated firing rates in the superficial layers during hits (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by the firing rate analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Broad- and narrow-spiking neurons trend toward elevated firing rates in the superficial layers during hits.
source: Broad- and narrow-spiking neurons in both the input and deep layers respond more to target stimuli in hit trials, and trend toward elevated firing rates in the superficial layers during hits (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by the firing rate analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The stimuli presented to the animals were identical for both hits and misses.
source: It is important to note that the stimuli presented to the animals were identical for both hits and misses.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design.

claim: The responses to the target stimuli occur early, and elevated firing in hits emerges at the time of expected V4 response latencies (70–100 ms).
source: Moreover, the responses to the target stimuli occur early, and elevated firing in hits emerges at the time of expected V4 response latencies (70–100 ms; Figure 3—figure supplement 3C), and thus cannot be attributed to elevated levels of firing due to subsequent saccade planning in these trials (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B; expected >200 ms; Steinmetz and Moore, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the timing analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C and comparison to expected saccade planning times.

claim: Elevated firing in hits cannot be attributed to elevated levels of firing due to subsequent saccade planning.
source: Moreover, the responses to the target stimuli occur early, and elevated firing in hits emerges at the time of expected V4 response latencies (70–100 ms; Figure 3—figure supplement 3C), and thus cannot be attributed to elevated levels of firing due to subsequent saccade planning in these trials (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B; expected >200 ms; Steinmetz and Moore, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of responses and comparison to expected saccade planning times.

claim: Lower baseline variability can enhance the ability of neurons to encode stimulus differences.
source: Variability in response reflects how reliably information is encoded by a neural population. Lower baseline variability can enhance the ability of neurons to encode stimulus differences.
evidence: This is established knowledge about neural coding.

claim: Broad-spiking units in the superficial layer exhibited lower Fano factor during the pre-stimulus period in hit trials.
source: We find that broad-spiking units in the superficial layer exhibited lower Fano factor during the pre-stimulus period in hit trials (0–60 ms before non-target stimulus onset, Figure 4B), indicating this population of neurons fired more reliably when the animal correctly detected the orientation change.
evidence: This is supported by the Fano factor analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Broad-spiking neurons in the superficial layer fired more reliably when the animal correctly detected the orientation change.
source: We find that broad-spiking units in the superficial layer exhibited lower Fano factor during the pre-stimulus period in hit trials (0–60 ms before non-target stimulus onset, Figure 4B), indicating this population of neurons fired more reliably when the animal correctly detected the orientation change.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Fano factor results.

claim: Broad-spiking neurons in other layers did not show lower Fano factor in hit trials.
source: This was not the case for broad-spiking neurons in other layers (Figure 4B) or narrow-spiking neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the Fano factor analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Narrow-spiking neurons did not show lower Fano factor in hit trials.
source: This was not the case for broad-spiking neurons in other layers (Figure 4B) or narrow-spiking neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the Fano factor analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Spike-LFP synchrony can reflect cortical processing and both within- and inter-areal coordination.
source: Spike-LFP synchrony can reflect cortical processing and both within- and inter-areal coordination (Fries, 2009; Fries et al., 2008; Siapas et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Deep-layer neurons exhibit reduced low-frequency phase-locking in hit trials than in misses.
source: Deep-layer neurons exhibit reduced low-frequency phase-locking in hit trials than in misses (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the PPC analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Desynchronization during hits is similar to prior reports of desynchronization due to the deployment of attention.
source: This desynchronization during hits is similar to prior reports of desynchronization due to the deployment of attention (Mitchell et al., 2009; Nandy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior literature.

claim: Interlaminar feed-forward population correlations were higher in hits than in misses in both the pre-stimulus and stimulus-evoked periods.
source: Interlaminar feed-forward population correlations were higher in hits than in misses in both the pre-stimulus and stimulus-evoked periods (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is supported by the CCA analysis shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: Feed-forward information flow through the column is more effective in hits than in misses.
source: This suggests that feed-forward information flow through the column is more effective in hits than in misses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the CCA results.

claim: Hit trials have greater interlaminar SSC compared to misses at almost all frequencies.
source: Overall, hit trials have greater interlaminar SSC compared to misses at almost all frequencies (Figure 7B and D).
evidence: This is supported by the SSC analysis shown in Figures 7B and 7D.

claim: In the pre-stimulus period, the strongest SSC difference between hits and misses was observed between the superficial and deep layers across all frequencies.
source: In the pre-stimulus period, the strongest SSC difference between hits and misses was observed between the superficial and deep layers across all frequencies (Figure 7B, middle panel).
evidence: This is supported by the SSC analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Greater synchrony of the output layers of the cortex during hit trials implies greater synchrony of the output layers of the cortex.
source: This implies greater synchrony of the output layers of the cortex during hit trials.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the SSC results.

claim: During the non-target stimulus-evoked period, greater SSC differences were found in pairs that involve the input layer.
source: In contrast, this pattern was directionally the same during the non-target stimulus-evoked period, but stronger in the other layer pairs, with greater SSC differences being found in pairs that involve the input layer (Figure 7D, top and bottom).
evidence: This is supported by the SSC analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Greater SSC in pairs involving the input layer during the stimulus-evoked period may reflect a higher degree of stimulus-driven feed-forward information propagation during hit trials.
source: This may reflect a higher degree of stimulus-driven feed-forward information propagation during hit trials.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the SSC results.

claim: There was a significant interaction effect of layer pair and time window on SSC.
source: When comparing across time (pre-stimulus vs non-target stimulus-evoked), layers, and frequency band, there was a significant interaction effect of layer pair and time window (three-way ANOVA, p = 0.0075).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from ANOVA analysis.

claim: Superficial firing rate, deep firing rate, and pupil diameter were not significant predictors in the GLM analysis.
source: Superficial firing rate, deep firing rate, and pupil diameter were not significant predictors (Supplementary file 1b, all p > 0.5).
evidence: This is supported by the GLM analysis results.

claim: Among the variables that could be estimated reliably on a single-trial basis, stable retinal images in the pre-target window are critical for behavioral performance.
source: This indicates that, among the variables that we could estimate reliably on a single-trial basis, stable retinal images in the pre-target window are critical for behavioral performance, and elevated firing in the input layer is the most reliable physiological signature of a perceived stimulus.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the GLM analysis results.

claim: Elevated firing in the input layer is the most reliable physiological signature of a perceived stimulus among single-trial measures.
source: This indicates that, among the variables that we could estimate reliably on a single-trial basis, stable retinal images in the pre-target window are critical for behavioral performance, and elevated firing in the input layer is the most reliable physiological signature of a perceived stimulus.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the GLM analysis results.

claim: Pupil diameter is strongly linked to arousal and alertness.
source: Pupil diameter is elevated in hit trials (Figure 2A–C; Figure 8A), and prior studies have shown that pupil diameter is strongly linked to arousal and alertness (Beatty and Lucero-Wagoner, 2000; Hess and Polt, 1964; Tang and Higley, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A state of higher arousal may contribute to improved sensory processing.
source: This provides evidence that a state of higher arousal may contribute to improved sensory processing.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pupil diameter findings.

claim: Stability of retinal images is critical for accurate discrimination at threshold.
source: The much lower hit rate in trials with a microsaccade preceding the target (Figure 2D; Figure 8A) and our GLM analysis show that stability of retinal images is critical for accurate discrimination at threshold.
evidence: This is supported by the microsaccade analysis and GLM results.

claim: Pupil diameter and microsaccade rate are unlikely to be reflecting the same phenomenon.
source: It is unlikely that these two measures are reflecting the same phenomenon, as there is a very weak correlation between them over the course of a trial (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the weak correlation between the two measures.

claim: There is a strong link between oculomotor control and attentional deployment.
source: There is a strong link between oculomotor control and attentional deployment (Moore and Zirnsak, 2017; Schafer and Moore, 2011; Moore and Fallah, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Almost all neural results reflect differences around the time of non-target stimulus presentations during which the monkeys maintained fixation at the center of the screen.
source: Almost all of our neural results reflect differences around the time of non-target stimulus presentations during which the monkeys maintained fixation at the center of the screen and, therefore, were hundreds of milliseconds prior to saccade planning and execution in the case of hit trials.
evidence: This is a statement about the timing of the neural measurements relative to behavior.

claim: Trials in which saccades were made to non-target stimuli were excluded from analysis.
source: Trials in which saccades were made to non-target stimuli were excluded from analysis, as were trials in which the monkey made a saccade to the target too soon after its presentation to have been a behavioral response to stimulus perception (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the data exclusion criteria.

claim: Trials in which the monkey made a saccade to the target too soon after its presentation to have been a behavioral response to stimulus perception were excluded from analysis.
source: Trials in which saccades were made to non-target stimuli were excluded from analysis, as were trials in which the monkey made a saccade to the target too soon after its presentation to have been a behavioral response to stimulus perception (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the data exclusion criteria.

claim: Firing rates diverge much earlier in response to target stimuli than would be consistent with the effects of saccade planning.
source: However, here too firing rates diverge much earlier, particularly in the input layer, than would be consistent with the effects of saccade planning (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; Steinmetz and Moore, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of firing rate differences and comparison to expected saccade planning times.

claim: Firing rates were normalized by contrast before performing the analyses reported in Figure 3 to control for potential effects of stimulus contrast.
source: To control for potential effects of stimulus contrast, firing rates were first normalized by contrast before performing the analyses reported in Figure 3.
evidence: This describes the data analysis method.

claim: For all results other than Figure 3, only non-target stimuli were considered, which had very minor differences in contrast (<1%) across hits and misses.
source: For all other results, we considered only non-target stimuli, which had very minor differences in contrast (<1%) across hits and misses.
evidence: This describes the data selection for analysis.

claim: Microsaccades directed toward a target stimulus reflect attention-related processing and performance.
source: A body of evidence (see Martinez-Conde et al., 2013, for review) suggests that microsaccades directed toward a target stimulus reflect attention-related processing and performance (Lowet et al., 2018; Engbert and Kliegl, 2003; Hafed and Clark, 2002; Gowen et al., 2007; Galfano et al., 2004; Pastukhov and Braun, 2010; Yu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Microsaccades directed toward the location of the eventual target may reflect elevated attentional deployment that can compensate for reduced sensitivity due to a higher incidence of microsaccades.
source: Microsaccades directed toward the location of the eventual target may reflect elevated attentional deployment that can compensate for reduced sensitivity due to a higher incidence of microsaccades.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the microsaccade direction findings.

claim: The electrophysiological findings and their laminar patterns associated with hit trials within a cued attention state mirror several previous findings that are associated with the deployment of covert spatial attention.
source: Our electrophysiological findings and their laminar patterns associated with hit trials within a cued attention state mirror several previous findings that are associated with the deployment of covert spatial attention.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings to prior literature.

claim: Attention has long been known to increase firing rates in V4.
source: Attention has long been known to increase firing rates in V4 (McAdams and Maunsell, 1999; Mitchell et al., 2007; Spitzer et al., 1988), and there is evidence that this increase occurs in all cortical layers in V4 (Nandy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: There is evidence that attention-related firing rate increases occur in all cortical layers in V4.
source: Attention has long been known to increase firing rates in V4 (McAdams and Maunsell, 1999; Mitchell et al., 2007; Spitzer et al., 1988), and there is evidence that this increase occurs in all cortical layers in V4 (Nandy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Attention reduces the variability in the firing of V4 neurons, and this reduction is thought to contribute to the improved information coding capacity of a population of neurons.
source: Attention reduces the variability in the firing of V4 neurons, and this reduction is thought to contribute to the improved information coding capacity of a population of neurons (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Mitchell et al., 2007; Mitchell et al., 2009; Nandy et al., 2017; Moreno-Bote et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The reduction in Fano factor among broad-spiking superficial-layer neurons in hit trials mirrors the effects of attention.
source: The reduction in Fano factor among broad-spiking superficial-layer neurons in hit trials mirrors the effects of attention (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings to prior literature on attention.

claim: Multiple lines of evidence suggest broad- and narrow-spiking correspond to putative excitatory and inhibitory neurons respectively.
source: Multiple lines of evidence suggest broad- and narrow-spiking correspond to putative excitatory and inhibitory neurons respectively.
evidence: This is a statement about the interpretation of cell type classification.

claim: Narrow-spiking neurons exhibit higher firing rates, which corresponds well with inhibitory interneuron properties.
source: Narrow-spiking neurons exhibit higher firing rates, which corresponds well with inhibitory interneuron (Connors and Gutnick, 1990; Nandy et al., 2017; McCormick et al., 1985; Contreras and Palmer, 2003; Foehring et al., 1991; Povysheva et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on neuron properties.

claim: Repolarization times in broad-spiking neurons are longer, as they are in excitatory pyramidal neurons.
source: Repolarization times in broad-spiking neurons are also longer, as they are in excitatory pyramidal neurons (McCormick et al., 1985; Nowak et al., 2003; Hasenstaub et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on neuron properties.

claim: Broad-spiking superficial layer neurons are putative projection neurons to downstream cortical areas.
source: Since these neurons are putative projection neurons to downstream cortical areas, this reduction in Fano factor may indicate increased reliability in stimulus encoding that could contribute to hits.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of cortical anatomy and the properties of broad-spiking neurons.

claim: Reduction in Fano factor among broad-spiking superficial-layer neurons may indicate increased reliability in stimulus encoding that could contribute to hits.
source: Since these neurons are putative projection neurons to downstream cortical areas, this reduction in Fano factor may indicate increased reliability in stimulus encoding that could contribute to hits.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Fano factor findings.

claim: The finding of lower variability in hit trials is in agreement with previous reports of higher variability in representations of unperceived stimuli in humans.
source: Our finding is also in agreement with previous reports of higher variability in representations of unperceived stimuli in humans (Schurger et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior literature.

claim: Synchronous neural activity appears to modulate perceptual and cognitive ability in a variety of contexts.
source: Synchronous neural activity appears to modulate perceptual and cognitive ability in a variety of contexts (Abbas et al., 2018; Fries et al., 2001; Rohenkohl et al., 2018; Worden et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The finding of reduced low-frequency phase-locking in deep-layer neurons during hits is consistent with prior studies that find an attention-mediated reduction in the power spectrum of the spike-triggered-averaged LFP.
source: This is consistent with prior studies that find an attention-mediated reduction in the power spectrum of the spike-triggered-averaged LFP (Fries et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior literature.

claim: A state of improved interlaminar information flow could be a result of neuromodulatory or top-down processes that maintain the cortex in a state of sustained depolarization corresponding to a state of higher arousal during hits.
source: This state of improved interlaminar information flow could be a result of neuromodulatory or top-down processes that maintain the cortex in a state of sustained depolarization corresponding to a state of higher arousal during hits (McCormick et al., 2020; McGinley et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the interlaminar correlation findings, with reference to prior literature.

claim: Increased superficial-deep coherence in the pre-stimulus period could be the result of neuromodulatory or top-down processes.
source: Increased superficial-deep coherence in the pre-stimulus period could be the result of the same neuromodulatory or top-down processes.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the SSC findings.

claim: Increased synchrony between the input layer and the output layers during the stimulus-evoked period provides further evidence of stronger information propagation through the cortical circuit, and hence with improved stimulus detection.
source: Increased synchrony between the input layer and the output layers during the stimulus-evoked period provides further evidence of stronger information propagation through the cortical circuit, and hence with improved stimulus detection (Marshel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the SSC findings, with reference to prior literature.

claim: Broad global synchrony or local correlated fluctuations may signal a default state of minimal processing or decreased information coding capacity.
source: In contrast to broad global synchrony or local correlated fluctuations, which may signal a default state of minimal processing or decreased information coding capacity (Mitchell et al., 2009; Steriade et al., 1993; Krosigk von et al., 1993; Zohary et al., 1994), these patterns of interlaminar coherence that we found suggest that successful perception at threshold is mediated by pathway-specific modulation of information flow through the laminar cortical circuit.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Successful perception at threshold is mediated by pathway-specific modulation of information flow through the laminar cortical circuit.
source: In contrast to broad global synchrony or local correlated fluctuations, which may signal a default state of minimal processing or decreased information coding capacity (Mitchell et al., 2009; Steriade et al., 1993; Krosigk von et al., 1993; Zohary et al., 1994), these patterns of interlaminar coherence that we found suggest that successful perception at threshold is mediated by pathway-specific modulation of information flow through the laminar cortical circuit.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the interlaminar coherence findings.

claim: Prior studies showing decreased correlations under attention typically do not contain laminar information.
source: Prior studies showing decreased correlations under attention typically do not contain laminar information (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Mitchell et al., 2009) or only consider decreased correlations within a layer (Nandy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about prior literature.

claim: The correlation and synchrony analyses presented in this study are interlaminar, which could reflect improved information processing in a column, similar to principles of communication across areas.
source: In contrast, the correlation and synchrony analyses presented here are interlaminar, which we expect could reflect improved information processing in a column, similar to principles of communication across areas (Semedo et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the current findings in the context of prior literature.

claim: Lower baseline variability among broad-spiking superficial layer neurons and decreased low-frequency synchronous activity in the deep layers could be indicative of improved capacity to encode sensory information.
source: Lower baseline variability among broad-spiking superficial layer neurons and decreased low-frequency synchronous activity in the deep layers could be indicative of improved capacity to encode sensory information.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Fano factor and PPC findings.

claim: Higher target-evoked firing rates and elevated interlaminar synchrony could enhance the propagation of encoded signals.
source: Higher target-evoked firing rates and elevated interlaminar synchrony could enhance the propagation of this encoded signal.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the firing rate and synchrony findings.

claim: Pre-stimulus baseline state differences are associated with enhanced cortical processing in the stimulus-evoked period.
source: These results associate pre-stimulus baseline state differences with enhanced cortical processing in the stimulus-evoked period.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the findings.

claim: van Vugt et al., 2018, recorded from three brain regions, V1, V4, and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, while a monkey performed a stimulus detection task at threshold.
source: van Vugt et al., 2018, recorded from three brain regions, V1, V4, and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, while a monkey performed a stimulus detection task at threshold.
evidence: This is a description of a prior study.

claim: van Vugt et al., 2018's work supports the model that feed-forward propagation of sensory information from the visual cortex to the PFC causes a non-linear 'ignition' of association areas resulting in conscious perception.
source: Their work supports the model that feed-forward propagation of sensory information from the visual cortex to the PFC causes a non-linear 'ignition' of association areas resulting in conscious perception (Dehaene and Changeux, 2011).
evidence: This is a description of the conclusions of a prior study.

claim: Herman et al., 2019, found that conscious human perception triggers a wave of activity propagation from occipital to frontal cortex while switching off default mode and other networks.
source: Herman et al., 2019, found that conscious human perception triggers a wave of activity propagation from occipital to frontal cortex while switching off default mode and other networks.
evidence: This is a description of the findings of a prior study.

claim: The current study provides insight into the functions of the cortical microcircuit at the columnar level that could reflect large-scale sweeping activity changes in perception.
source: Our study provides insight into the functions of the cortical microcircuit at the columnar level that could reflect these large-scale sweeping activity changes in perception.
evidence: This is a statement about the contribution of the current study.

claim: During spontaneous activity, the state of elevated arousal and eye position stability during hits is manifested by increased interlaminar synchrony between the superficial and deep layers, which is proposed to be due to top-down influences.
source: During spontaneous activity, the state of elevated arousal and eye position stability during hits (Figure 8A) is manifested by increased interlaminar synchrony between the superficial and deep layers (Figure 8B, thicker orange arrows), which we propose is due to top-down influences.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the findings, presented in the conceptual model.

claim: Decreased firing variability in broad-spiking neurons in the superficial layer is predicted to be caused by a lower variability in membrane potential closer to the action potential threshold among these neurons.
source: We predict that decreased firing variability in broad-spiking neurons in the superficial layer is caused by a lower variability in membrane potential closer to the action potential threshold among these neurons (Figure 8B, inset).
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the Fano factor findings.

claim: Elevated feed-forward propagation in the stimulus-evoked period and a membrane potential closer to action potential threshold could both contribute to higher firing rates in the output layers of the cortex.
source: Elevated feed-forward propagation in the stimulus-evoked period (Figure 8C) and a membrane potential closer to action potential threshold could both contribute to higher firing rates in the output layers of the cortex (Figure 8C, inset), and are indicative of greater fidelity of stimulus processing in hits.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the findings, presented in the conceptual model.

claim: Higher firing rates in the output layers are indicative of greater fidelity of stimulus processing in hits.
source: Elevated feed-forward propagation in the stimulus-evoked period (Figure 8C) and a membrane potential closer to action potential threshold could both contribute to higher firing rates in the output layers of the cortex (Figure 8C, inset), and are indicative of greater fidelity of stimulus processing in hits.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the findings, presented in the conceptual model.

claim: Physiological differences in the laminar microcircuit likely contribute to successful perceptual discrimination at threshold.
source: These physiological differences in the laminar microcircuit likely contribute to successful perceptual discrimination at threshold.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Data was collected over 32 sessions (23 sessions in Monkey A, 9 in Monkey C).
source: Data was collected over 32 sessions (23 sessions in Monkey A, 9 in Monkey C), yielding a total of 413 single units (146 narrow-spiking, 267 broad-spiking) and 296 multi-unit clusters.
evidence: This is a description of the dataset.

claim: A total of 413 single units (146 narrow-spiking, 267 broad-spiking) and 296 multi-unit clusters were recorded.
source: Data was collected over 32 sessions (23 sessions in Monkey A, 9 in Monkey C), yielding a total of 413 single units (146 narrow-spiking, 267 broad-spiking) and 296 multi-unit clusters.
evidence: This is a description of the dataset.

claim: Per session unit yield was considerably higher in Monkey C compared to Monkey A, resulting in a roughly equal contribution of both monkeys toward the population data.
source: Per session unit yield was considerably higher in Monkey C compared to Monkey A, resulting in a roughly equal contribution of both monkeys toward the population data.
evidence: This is a description of the dataset.
